Header: Spodoptera exempta Temch in Amharic language, Gerii in Oromiffa language

Prevention: Amaranthus and grassy weeds since they are food for young armyworm caterpillars
Plough and harrow field thoroughly after harvest or before planting to expose pupae from the soil to natural enemies and desiccation
Note that ploughing reduces water retention of soil and destroys soil structure.
Crop rotation has little effect on the pest because the adult moths are mobile and can immigrate to new maize fields.
You may rotate maize with non-cereals such as legumes (haricot and soya bean, cow and pigeon peas).
Avoid nearby planting or rotation with hosts such as teff, barely, oat, millet, sorghum, wheat
Monitoring: Monitoring
Monitor from germination till late vegetative maize
Armyworm moth: stout-bodied, 1 ½ to 2 cm long, wing 3 cm.
Forewings dark brown with grey-dark markings.
Hind wings white with dark edges
Place 1 sex pheromone trap / 100 m around maize.
When more than 30 moths a trapped / week and rainfall is >5mm on any day / week and maize is < knee high, then the main armyworm period may start.
Get armyworm forecasts from trained farmers.
Check weekly for caterpillars and feeding on leaves.
Check for caterpillars late evening/early morning; as they feed at night and hide under debris or at the base of plants during the day.2
Young caterpillars are green. yellow and brown with longitudinal stripes.
Length is ½ cm
They sometimes hang threads below the leaves.
Young caterpillars feed by scraping the surface of young leaves leaving a thin layer known as windows
Older caterpillars (1 to 2.5 cm) are velvety-black on the upper body with green, black, yellow, and white lateral stripes.
Inverted
V-shaped mark on head.
Fall armyworm looks similar has four dark spots forming a square at the end of the back.
Older armyworms bite and cut through leaves
Look for chewed leaves making the crop look ragged
Consider green control when 5 – 10% leaf damage on about half of plants at young caterpillars.
But at older caterpillars, direct control maybe more urgent.
When 15 – 25 % of leaf damage per plant consider chemical control
At >30 % damage and old caterpillar stage, action may be too late
Direct Control: Hand pick caterpillars, destroy them by crushing or feed to chickens or ducks.
Dig a 30 cm deep trench with vertical sides around the field to trap marching caterpillars.
Put a handful of sand (mixed with lime or ash), sawdust or soil in the whorl of the attacked plants to repel the caterpilars.
Encourage natural enemies such as birds, toads, lizards and spiders by planting trees and shrubs.
